newsitem.title: USA: IMF sees growth, set to resume Russia loan payments.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees growth, set to resume Russia loan payments.

text.p: The head of the IMF said Thursday that lending to Russia could resume next month, but officials in Moscow cast doubt on whether they actually needed the cash.

IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus told a news conference that the International Monetary Fund was likely to approve Russia's 1997 economic programme next month, and that disbursements could restart "immediately after that."

"If this programme is continued, as it is expected to be, until the end of this century, Russia will enter the next millennium with a solid, sustained base for growth and the improved living standards of the population," he said.
Russian gross domestic product has declined stubbornly since Moscow launched its economic reform programme in 1992, but the IMF predicts GDP growth of 3 percent this year.

"The government's fiscal position remains fragile, with revenue collection particularly weak, but recent indicators suggest that the long-awaited recovery of output may materialise in 1997," the IMF's World Economic Outlook said.
Itar-Tass news agency said on Wednesday that a draft 1998 budget forecast 3 percent to 5 percent growth next year.

The IMF, which is reviewing the state of the Russian economy each month, has not paid any of this year's monthly instalments of the three-year, $10 billion loan because it is worried about the country's low tax revenues.
Each monthly payment, or tranche, is worth about $330 million and Russia has included IMF loans of $3.65 billion in this year's budget.
A team of IMF experts is in Moscow this week to assess the latest figures and finish work on the 1997 programme.

"I am reasonably certain that we can present the second tranche of the three-year programme to the approval of the (IMF) board in May and that disbursement would restart immediately after that," Camdessus said.

Russian officials are determined to resolve the revenue crunch by cutting spending levels across the board and they have played down the possibility that delays to the IMF payments could cause problems.
"Today the IMF loans do not play even a fifth of the role for Russia which they played two years ago," First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais told reporters in Moscow.

"The IMF loans continue to remain cheap ... but in principle we can borrow money for a slightly higher price on the European private markets," Chubais, who is also Finance Minister and in charge of Russian economic reforms, added.
"Private investors recognise today that we are a reliable country, and our room for manoeuvre has widened sharply."
Russia has already issued two Eurobonds and a third is due in the coming months.
Chubais said he did not intend to discuss either the delayed tranches of the IMF loan or the 1997 programme when he visits Washington this week for the IMF spring meetings.
"There is an IMF mission here and the final technical details are in the process of being worked out. Frankly, I am not concerned," he said.
Camdessus said he had been impressed with Russia's new ministers -- including Chubais -- during a visit to Moscow at the start of this month.
"I was very impressed with the quality of the new government," he said. "It is quite refreshing to see such a strong determination to address squarely the basic issues."
